name: Wright County

actions.title: Emergency Data Center Moratorium (Interim Ordinance 26-2)
actions.summary: Wright County Board unanimously adopted Interim Ordinance 26-2, halting new data center applications in all county townships for up to one year while officials develop zoning regulations on setbacks and operating conditions.

contextBlurb: Wright County became the first Minnesota county to enact an emergency data center moratorium, driven largely by community opposition to two proposals totaling over four million square feet near Monticello. All 14 speakers at the May 19 public hearing supported the moratorium, citing concerns about aquifer protection, noise, and property values. The county board plans to form a stakeholder work group, similar to prior efforts on solar farms and gravel pits, to draft a permanent ordinance.

name: Eagan (Dakota County)

actions.title: One-Year Data Center Moratorium — Size and Proximity Restrictions
actions.summary: Eagan City Council approved a one-year moratorium blocking new data centers requiring more than 20 MW of electricity or upgrades to existing sites above 9 MW within 500 feet of residential areas, making it the first Minnesota city to enact such a size-and-proximity-based pause.

actions.title: Legal Challenge by Eagan Capital (Swervo Affiliate)
actions.summary: A developer affiliated with Swervo filed suit against Eagan challenging the moratorium as unlawful, arguing it blocks conversion of a former Unisys facility at 3199 Pilot Knob Road into a multi-tenant colocation site.

contextBlurb: Eagan is believed to be the first Minnesota city to enact a data center moratorium based on power capacity and proximity to homes, setting a template that several other cities subsequently followed. The city has at least four existing or in-development data centers but acted preemptively before a new large-scale application was filed. The moratorium now faces a legal challenge from a developer seeking to convert a former Unisys facility, with Eagan stating it will vigorously defend the policy.

name: Inver Grove Heights (Dakota County)

actions.title: One-Year Data Center Moratorium
actions.summary: The Inver Grove Heights City Council approved a one-year moratorium on data center construction in a 3-2 vote despite a developer threatening up to $150 million in litigation damages over its proposed 54,000 sq ft facility on the former Travel Tags site.

contextBlurb: Inver Grove Heights initiated moratorium proceedings in May 2026 after a Fortress Investment Group–backed developer proposed a 5 MW data center on the former Travel Tags site on Carmen Avenue. The city faced a race against a statutory 120-day application deadline of July 1, 2026, and the developer refused to grant an extension. A split council ultimately approved the one-year moratorium despite legal threats, joining a growing wave of Dakota County communities imposing construction pauses.

name: Minneapolis (Hennepin County)

actions.title: Six-Month Partial Data Center Moratorium
actions.summary: The Minneapolis City Council voted 8-5 to enact a six-month moratorium on new or expanded data centers outside downtown and on downtown facilities exceeding 350,000 sq ft, running through November 21, 2026.

actions.title: Proposed Zoning Ordinance Amendments for Data Centers
actions.summary: Nine council members gave notice of intent to co-author zoning code amendments that could limit data center size, require conditional-use permits, and potentially ban centers from some districts, with a draft expected by October–November 2026.

contextBlurb: Minneapolis joined the growing list of Minnesota cities imposing data center pauses, scaled back from an original one-year citywide ban to a five-month partial moratorium that exempts smaller downtown facilities to protect the city's struggling commercial tax base. Council members directing the study cited concerns over cumulative energy use, water consumption, and environmental-justice impacts on communities of color. A staff report on environmental impacts, permitting, and utility infrastructure is due in early fall 2026.

name: Carver (Carver County)

actions.title: Interim Ordinance — Data Center Moratorium
actions.summary: The City of Carver adopted an interim ordinance imposing a one-year moratorium prohibiting data center construction or expansion citywide while the planning commission studies and recommends zoning amendments.

contextBlurb: Carver enacted one of the earliest Minnesota city-level data center moratoriums in April 2026, declaring data centers a prohibited use for the duration of the interim ordinance under Minnesota Statutes §462.355. The ordinance authorizes the planning commission to study whether and how the zoning code should be amended, with the moratorium expiring upon adoption of permanent data center zoning language or after one year. Carver's action was cited as a model by subsequent Minnesota communities considering similar pauses.

name: Monticello (Wright County)

actions.title: Data Center Planned Unit Development (DCPUD) Ordinance
actions.summary: Monticello City Council approved a dedicated data center zoning ordinance creating a Data Center PUD district with restrictions including setbacks from residential areas and a requirement that residents bear no financial costs from data center infrastructure.

actions.title: MCEA Lawsuit Over Environmental Review (AUAR) Adequacy
actions.summary: The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy sued Monticello, alleging the city used an overly general environmental review process for the 550-acre Monticello Tech LLC data center campus proposal.

contextBlurb: Monticello has been at the epicenter of Minnesota's data center debate, with two massive proposals—a 3 million sq ft campus on 550 acres and a 1.3 million sq ft facility near Bertram Chain of Lakes—prompting heated council meetings and protests. In April 2026 the city enacted a bespoke Data Center PUD ordinance establishing setback rules and financial-protection provisions for residents. The city faces a lawsuit from the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy alleging the environmental review was inadequate for facilities of this scale.

name: St. Louis County

actions.title: Zoning Reclassification Review — Data Centers Removed from Industrial Class Two
actions.summary: St. Louis County Planning Commission reversed a proposed reclassification that would have moved data centers into the industrial use category, instead withdrawing the amendment and opening public workshops to develop clearer data center zoning standards.

contextBlurb: St. Louis County's planning debate was heavily influenced by community opposition to a proposed Google data center in the city of Hermantown, even though the county has no direct jurisdiction over that project. After pulling back a proposed industrial reclassification of data centers following strong public pushback, the county planning commission moved into a series of public workshops to gather input on appropriate zoning standards. Residents and commissioners acknowledged the existing ordinance language was not written with modern hyperscale data centers in mind.

name: Carlton County

actions.title: Interim Ordinance — Data Center Moratorium Under Consideration
actions.summary: The Carlton County Board of Commissioners advanced a proposed one-year interim ordinance that would pause data center construction countywide while officials complete a comprehensive land use plan review, with a final vote and public hearing expected in August 2026.

contextBlurb: Carlton County advanced a data center moratorium proposal in early July 2026 following pressure from the Carlton County Land Stewards, a grassroots group that previously organized against Enbridge's Line 3 pipeline. The board noted that the county's existing zoning ordinance does not contemplate data centers as a land use, creating regulatory gaps. The county's interest was partly driven by awareness of the nearby Hermantown Google data center controversy, and by reports that Silver Brook Township on the county's eastern edge is being evaluated as a potential data center site.
